title: Where does the international student deficit really lie?
summary: International students are often treated as financial assets rather than pedagogic partners. Sumeya Loonat sets out four lenses for moving beyond the deficit model
full_text:
In 2019 I moved from teaching English language at De Montfort University into my current role more broadly supporting international students in our business school.

The last seven years have opened my eyes to the actual lived realities of international students’ experiences of studying in the UK, to see those experiences rather more holistically than merely through the lens of their linguistic proficiencies.

As I learned and developed in my own understanding of, and approaches to, the international student experience, I came to appreciate the importance of such learning and development for all staff involved in teaching and supporting international students. The importance of ensuring that all staff are equipped with the skills and mindset essential to support the enhancement of this sometimes underserved area of the higher education experience became clear.

I found myself engaged in frequent conversations with colleagues across our sector which returned repeatedly to the same point: an acknowledgement of a lack of practical approaches underway to challenge what can be seen as the “international student deficit model,” and to develop ways to address the issues underlying it.

This was because – as I came to see – one of the more deleterious clichés of British higher education has been the common assumption that international students can be defined by a series of deficits, by the assumption that they lack English language abilities, critical thinking skills, and familiarity with British academic conventions.

The wrong assumption

As academics we’re of course trained to recognise and interrogate preconceptions promulgated without the evidence necessary to support them.

Yet this one somehow relentlessly persists. We’re all aware that our understanding of the world can be led dangerously astray by stereotypes – and indeed, in this case, a tired old stereotype will start to melt away as soon as we look at what’s actually taking place.

When we come to examine the shortcomings of the international student experience, it emerges that the most significant area of deficit may not in fact lie with the students themselves at all.

It may instead lie in the approaches taken by that colleague who lacks an appropriate understanding of their students’ educational histories or with an institution that provides its staff with minimal professional development to support students with different educational and cultural backgrounds. It may lie with a curriculum that treats western academic conventions as universal, incontrovertible and sacrosanct or assessment frameworks that were never designed with diverse learners in mind.

Partners, not pennies

In partnership with colleagues from the University of Wolverhampton, the University of Manchester and Manchester Metropolitan University, our QAA-funded Collaborative Enhancement Project has charted these possibilities and has proposed a route towards a more ethical and expansive model of international student pedagogy.

We started by convening a series of workshops involving staff from our four institutions to find out what was really going on in our approaches to international students and how we might improve them. We created these spaces to share good practice – from ways to design inductions to the co-creation of assessment briefs – and involved a broad range of colleagues, from leaders of our international teams to senior academic practitioners, coming together in a spirit of constructive candour to explore the differences we might make.

One point that was particularly striking from the outset was that the participants in these workshops consistently identified the ways in which institutions frame international students as financial assets rather than pedagogic partners.

Unprompted by our facilitators, the term “cash cows” was used directly and repeatedly by members of staff – colleagues stressed that they found this framing at the same time accurate and deeply uncomfortable.

It seems inevitable that the financial logic of their recruitment shapes the conditions in which international students arrive, the speed at which they are expected to integrate, the support made available to them, and the ways in which their presence, expectations, and needs are communicated to academic staff.

We’ve reached the conclusion that when an institution that recruits students as a part of its financial strategy and then tasks individual educators with the consequences of that strategy is producing structural injustice, not a pedagogic problem.

When an institution recruits a student from overseas, taking significant fees, giving them a place that may shape their future and making promises about the education and experience they will receive, it incurs an obligation that goes well beyond logistics. What is required – and this is the fundamental obligation which that institution places upon itself – is that the provider ensures a sustained, resourced, and embedded commitment to the conditions in which that international student can genuinely thrive.

Four ways forward

This has led us to emphasise an urgent pedagogical and ethical imperative to reframe UK higher education’s traditional “international student deficit” narrative.

In order to address this, we’ve developed four interconnected lenses for examining both institutional provision and individual practice. We’ve done this by seeing these issues through the positioning and construction of the international student, the epistemological centring of western academic conventions in curricula, a reflexive examination of the assumptions underpinning pedagogic practice, and an interrogation of the structural conditions that make inclusive practice impossible. This includes workload pressures, large class sizes, late arrivals, a lack of professional development and the financial logic of mass international student recruitment.

Published alongside an audit toolkit and a guide to inclusive practices, our project has also proposed a set of principles designed to underpin ways to support staff in enhancing the international student experience.

Before you teach, recognise who is in the room as individuals with histories, knowledge, and perspectives, not as a category defined by fee status or visa type

When a student appears to struggle, ask where the deficit actually lies – honest diagnosis is the precondition for honest intervention

Act where you can, and name what constrains you: inclusive practice requires both individual commitment and institutional change

Centre the voices of international students: decisions about curriculum, pedagogy, and support should be informed by the actual experiences of the students they are intended to serve

The duty of care towards international students does not begin at induction, it begins when recruitment promises are made

See what international students bring rather than what they lack, and to build the structures that allow those contributions to be recognised and valued

It’s only by valuing all of our students as unique individuals and unique learners, rather than as agglomerations of income-generating assets and recognising the richness of diverse perspectives and experiences that all our students bring that we can begin to build properly equitable and effective learning processes. And in doing so we can share the benefits underpinned and enriched by all those who contribute to the learning experience.

That’s an important lesson for educators, institutions, and policymakers.

And also, perhaps, for all those who in the mass media and public life who have sought to represent the presence of international students in the UK as a problem – or, at best, as an increasingly essential income stream – rather than as a rich cultural and intellectual resource we should endeavour most effectively to utilise, support, sustain, and celebrate.

This project has crucially been a collaborative effort, and as such has highlighted the vital importance of collaboration and co-creation in this space. It has recognised that a hostile environment – one which presumes problems and deficits – helps no one, and that partnership and belonging benefits all.

title: Some students arrive to find the door to belonging already shut
summary: Radhika Sharma has followed five students' experiences from the Global South and finds belonging is a design choice that the sector keeps getting wrong
full_text:
We tend to talk about belonging as something students grow into.

Give them a term or two, a couple of societies, and a friendly flat mate, and they will settle. The five students I spent a year listening to described something closer to chasing a bus that has already pulled away from the stop.

I followed five students from the Global South at a Scottish university across one academic year. They kept journals in whatever form suited them, prayers, lists, fragments, long entries written at two in the morning, set down on their own terms without me deciding what counted. I did not want their experiences filtered through my questions before they had a chance to name them in their own words.

What they produced was not a list of grievances. It was a quietly life account of how a university decides who gets to belong, and when.

The belonging window

The sharpest pattern was the student could see from inside their own year.

The opening fortnight of term carries an enormous social load. Friendships form easily because everyone is equally adrift, society sign-ups happen in a rush, group chats assemble overnight, and the cost of saying hello to a stranger is briefly almost nothing.

I came to think of this as a belonging window. It opens for everyone at once and closes for everyone at once. The real question is who can be in the building while it is open.

Roma, an undergraduate from Nigeria, arrived three weeks into term. Her visa, her flights and her family circumstances did not rearrange themselves to fit the university calendar. By the time she reached her first lecture the benches had their regulars, the cohort chat was already trading in-jokes she could not follow, and the easy welcome of week one had set into something she now had to break into from the outside.

She had dreamed of arriving. She arrived to find the place had carried on without her. And this is not a story about one student, and that is the point. Late arrival is produced, and it is produced unevenly.

Visa backlogs, the price of an international flight, caring responsibilities that cannot be paused, programmes that start off cycle, all of these land hardest on the students our access statements say we most want to reach. The window shuts at the same moment for everyone. Only some students ever had a fair chance of getting through it.

Coming into focus

Once you see the window, other things sharpen into view.

Every student in the study described a constant background calculation about how much of themselves was safe to show.

Shiv, a postgraduate from India, arrived from a classroom culture built on respect for expertise into British seminars that reward interruption and pushback. He could read the new rule easily enough. Playing it while also wondering whether his accent had already cost him the benefit of the doubt was a second job running underneath the first.

Erica, a doctoral researcher from Ghana, weighed every seminar contribution as a Black African woman in a room that did not extend her the authority that it extended others without thinking.

For Shiv there was a further layer, the careful management of an LGBTQ+ identity that was celebrated in some campus spaces and dangerous to reveal near the co-nationals who kept in touch with home. And it all runs at the same time as the actual studying rather than in some separate, quieter hour.

Filling in the gaps

What moved me the most was what students built when the institution came up short.

Erica had a church that expected her each week, a diaspora group that swapped recipes and hardwon advice about the university’s own systems, and a community organisation that took her research seriously.

Nya’s days were held together by the religious society and the rhythm of Ramadan, which gave her a structure the rest of campus rarely offered. Roma found the chaplaincy, warm and undemanding, where a hot chocolate came with no requirement to explain herself first. We usually file these under cultural preference, the nice extras that sit beside the real support. I think that reading is backwards.

Students built these circuits because the official ones were hard to reach or not matched to their lives, and the circuits worked because they offered the one thing formal provision so often withholds, which is repetition.

Somewhere you can return to and be known without translating yourself at the door. Read properly, these student-made systems are not just curiosities but the clearest blueprint we have for what our own support keeps missing.

It really is the little things

The other side of this is how little it took to turn a student’s year around.

A tutor saying a contribution was interesting, right after it had been delivered in a shaky voice and a strong accent. A laptop loan finally approved after weeks of unexplained refusals. These sound minor, and that is exactly why they matter.

For someone who has been bracing to be heard as less capable before they have even spoken, a small signal that their voice carries knowledge rather than getting in its way is a genuine redistribution of authority. Repeated across a year, these moments gather into something that starts to feel like standing.

So what would it mean to take this seriously?

It would mean designing for repetition rather than pouring everything into the first fortnight, so that the chances to connect, to be recognised and to find support are spread across the whole year. It would mean building a real welcome for students who arrive off cycle, instead of leaving them to reconstruct week one alone in week four. It would mean recognising and resourcing the student communities already doing the heaviest belonging work, rather than admiring them from a distance. And it would mean clearer support pathways so that a student does not need “insider” knowledge of which door to knock on to reach help they are entitled to.

Underneath all of it the students were not just having experiences for me to interpret. They were theorising their own lives, in lines like being present is not the same as belonging. That is knowledge, produced from inside conditions no outside observer can reach, and it deserves to be treated as knowledge rather than as raw feeling waiting for an academic to make sense of it.

Belonging is not a personality trait some students happen to have and others lack.

It is something we hand out, on a schedule, through a hundred small design choices about timing, tone and who gets recognised. The good news buried in these journals is that if we are the ones distributing it, then we are also the ones who can distribute it more fairly. We just have to stop treating the door as if it opens itself.

The post WEEKEND READING: Why specialist institutions are central to the UK’s economic future appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Penny Macbeth, Chair of the Specialist Institution Forum, Director and Principal of The Glasgow School of Art and Nadine Patel, UUK Policy Adviser (specialist institutions forum) & Lead for Conservatoires UK.

Earlier this year, we gathered at the Royal College of Music for the Universities UK Specialist Institutions Forum (SIF) dinner, an evening that brought together leaders from across our unique and diverse community of specialist providers. We were honoured to be joined by Baroness Smith, Minister for Higher Education, alongside Universities UK President Professor Malcolm Press and colleagues from UUK.

The evening created a valuable space for candid reflection on the extraordinary contribution of specialist institutions and it left us firmly convinced that, now more than ever, our higher education specialist community must find its voice and advocate for its impact.

What makes us different is exactly the point

Specialist institutions span an extraordinary range of disciplines: health, the creative industries, science, engineering, technology and humanities. Some of us founded our disciplinary fields, others are custodians of subjects that would simply disappear without us. All of us are at the forefront of change in our sectors.

What unites us is not size or subject matter. It is depth and focus.

Because we concentrate on a single discipline or a closely related cluster of fields, we can do things that the comprehensive university cannot. Teaching is intensive, often one-to-one or in small groups. Facilities are professional grade: studios, laboratories – environments that replicate the real world from day one. ur ties to industry and the wider economy are integral to how we teach and research. All of us are innovators, shaping and working at the forefront of future developments.

At the Royal College of Music, we saw this model brought to life: cutting-edge simulation technologies that can be applied by organisations as varied as the Football Association and the United Nations, alongside interdisciplinary partners like Imperial College. Together, they have created a learning environment that prepares participants not only to master the concept of performance (whether as a public speaker, musician, sportsperson or a surgeon,), but also to do so under pressure and sustain long-term careers. Across the specialist institutions, this intensity translates into graduates who are not only employable but profession ready.

Partnership is integral to innovation.

As colleagues from Cranfield University put it plainly: partnership is not an add-on. It is foundational to everything we do.

In specialist institutions, the boundary between academia and industry is deliberately porous. Staff move between the two, industry partners co-design curricula and students engage with real-world challenges from their very first year. The result is skills provision that is not catching up with the economy; it is anticipating it.

Across SIF the evidence of this is everywhere. Long-standing industrial collaborations shaping advanced technical education. Creative partnerships that keep curricula agile in sectors that shift faster than any policy cycle can track. Global connections that extend UK expertise and influence far beyond our shores. These relationships are what keep specialist provision relevant. They are what make our graduates not merely employable, but immediately, demonstrably valuable.

Baroness Smith was direct about this: it is a story we must tell more clearly and more loudly. She is right. We have been too modest for too long.

Local roots. Global reach. Both matter.

There is a persistent misconception that specialist institutions are niche, impressive within their field, but peripheral to the wider economic and civic picture. The reality is the complete opposite.

Institutions like the Royal Northern College of Music and the University of the Creative Arts are not just globally ranked; they are anchor institutions in their regions. They drive local employment, build talent pipelines and sustain cultural and economic ecosystems that would be poorer without them. They reach students from underrepresented backgrounds, often across large regional geographies, and they work hand in hand with schools, health services and community organisations.

At the same time, they are outward-facing and globally ambitious. As colleagues from Trinity Laban made clear, international students do not dilute the domestic experience, they enrich it. They bring perspectives, networks and professional connections that make every student better prepared for the world they are about to enter.

Local anchors and global players: we are both, simultaneously.

Innovation and outcomes

Innovation in a specialist institution is applied. It is practice-based. It is interdisciplinary by design. And it is, time and again, connected directly to real-world challenges that matter.

The Royal College of Art brings together design, health, artificial intelligence and sustainability in ways that would be impossible in a more siloed environment. The Royal Veterinary College navigates the genuine complexities of scaling research and commercialisation in a field where the stakes – animal welfare, food security, public health – could not be higher. These are not peripheral research activities. They create jobs, seed new industries and generate solutions to problems society cannot afford to leave unsolved.

As the vice chancellor of the RCA put it with characteristic precision:

Our graduates do not just get jobs, they create them.

But here is what we must also say clearly: this kind of innovation requires room to experiment. Current funding and regulatory frameworks too often act as barriers where they should be enablers. That is not a minor irritant, it is a structural problem with real consequences for the UK. This manifests itself regionally, but also more explicitly in the devolved nations where our specialists navigate both devolved and UK wide policies and priorities, often advocating for a more joined-up approach to major economic strategies. A failure to fully realise the potential here will inhibit the UK’s capacity to innovate to its full potential.

The skills gap we are closing and the policy gap we cannot afford to ignore

One of the exchanges of the evening centred on lifelong learning and upskilling. The government’s ambitions in this space are real and right, and specialist institutions are already doing the work.

We produce graduates who go on to become freelancers, entrepreneurs and portfolio professionals, individuals who will need to keep developing their skills throughout careers that will look nothing like the linear paths of previous generations. We are built for this. We understand it from the inside.

And yet, as many institutions highlighted, a significant disconnect remains. In England, many Level 7 and 8 providers cannot currently engage fully with mechanisms like the Lifelong Learning Entitlement. As it stands, the LLE is focussedon undergraduate and higher technical education, so a mature learner seeking to advance their skills through qualifications such as Master’s degrees or PhDs are largely excluded from the core entitlement. The ambition to support advanced skills development is stated clearly in policy. The frameworks to actually deliver it, for some specialist institutions, are not yet there.

This is not a complaint. In fact it could be a precise and solvable problem if we name it clearly enough and if policymakers are willing to engage with the details. The question is whether we meet that willingness with the specificity it deserves.

Now it is time for us to shout louder

Our contribution is already central to UUK’s future universities programme, setting out a bold vision for higher education’s contribution socially and economically. The Minister’s challenge to us was unambiguous: shout louder. Be more explicit about our contribution and make the employability, skills, civic and regional impact visible with data and evidence.

We hear that challenge and we accept it.

title: ‘Tiger mum’ Lucy Powell on Labour’s vocational skills drive: ‘It’s about ambition for everybody’
summary:
New education secretary says it is ‘false trade-off’ by critics to suggest schools cannot pursue academic excellence alongside technical skills

Lucy Powell has said she wants to be an ambitious “tiger mum” for all young people, whatever their route through education, after the government was accused of dumbing down England’s schools with plans to create more vocational routes.

The new education secretary said secondary pupils should be able to pursue academic excellence as well as high-quality vocational training, and it was a “false trade-off” to suggest schools could not provide both.

full_text:
Lucy Powell has said she wants to be an ambitious “tiger mum” for all young people, whatever their route through education, after the government was accused of dumbing down England’s schools with plans to create more vocational routes.

The new education secretary said secondary pupils should be able to pursue academic excellence as well as high-quality vocational training, and it was a “false trade-off” to suggest schools could not provide both.

In an interview with the Guardian, Powell said she did not have “lower ambition” for those children following technical routes, and her critics – including Michael Gove, the former Tory education secretary – should recognise that their approach had left too many behind.

Andy Burnham told schools across England this week to adapt their curriculums to the needs of local businesses, as part of a drive to make technical and vocational skills as valued as academic qualifications and help tackle the jobs crisis for young people.

Powell said: “I absolutely don’t want schools to dumb down. My kids might say I’m a tiger mum. You know, I’m a tiger mum for all our kids – every single child that’s in our education system achieving excellence, achieving what they can do.”

Powell said those arguing against a focus on vocational education were making a “false trade-off” by framing Labour’s plans as a choice between knowledge and skills. “What I’m not going to oversee is some kind of lower ambition for some kids. It’s about ambition for everybody.”

Most of the criticism of her approach has come from Tory politicians who oversaw the system for years. “They have to take some responsibility for creating … a system that has left over a million young people now not in education, training or employment. The current approach has left too many behind,” Powell said.

However, she acknowledged that headteachers were concerned about extra pressure on their budgets to provide vocational routes, saying she was “very conscious” of school funding, which took a hit during the austerity years. She insisted any specific new proposals would be fully funded.

With many teachers struggling, and strikes potentially looming, Powell said she wanted a constructive relationship with the unions, and the government was already making changes to help ease the pressure. “What I’ll say to teachers is ‘work with me’,” she said.

Powell has been under pressure since she took over the brief to row back on plans made by her predecessor, Bridget Phillipson, to overhaul the special educational needs and disabilities system (Send), in particular limiting education, health and care plans (EHCP) to pupils with the “most complex needs”.

Powell signalled that she would stick to the plans, while accepting that the issue was creating worry and anxiety for many parents. “We can reassure them, because this is about tilting the system so that you don’t have to fight tooth and nail. That you get much earlier help,” she said.

Pressed on Labour’s election pledge to recruit 6,500 teachers, which has since been watered down, she suggested the government was doing well against a lower target, and that a sharp drop in primary numbers reflected falling rolls in schools.

Asked about private schools, Powell took a less adversarial approach than her predecessor, saying it was up to parents to make their own decisions about where they sent their children. “I’m not here to worry about private schools. I’m here to worry about state schools,” she said.

Powell added that she would be spending a significant amount of time at the No 10 North outpost in her central Manchester constituency. The DfE’s third biggest office, housing 1,100 civil servants, is also based in the city.

She batted away suggestions she was unhappy not to have been appointed deputy prime minister by Burnham, saying they had agreed she would continue to play a central role in Labour’s political direction as education secretary.

There had been no purge of the Starmerites, she added, saying the new cabinet was representative of people from across the party, and that, in contrast, the last cabinet had been too narrow. “That was one of the issues for Keir towards the end. His government wasn’t necessarily one of all the traditions.”

Powell also criticised Starmer’s government for focusing too much on the Reform threat rather than Labour’s own plan for the country. “What most people wanted to know was not what we thought about other political parties, but what were we doing? What were we about? What has been refreshing over the last week or two, is being on the front foot. Every day you’re on the front foot is a day you’re winning.”

She insisted that despite multiple spending pledges in Burnham’s first fortnight in office, all policy announcements were funded, with the prime minister and his chancellor, John Healey, “quite prudent and careful” about this.

title: Two universities merge to create the UK’s first ‘super-university’
summary: The new London and South East University Group has more than 50,000 students and four campuses across London, Medway and Kent
full_text:
The Universities of Kent and Greenwich have merged to create what they describe as the UK’s first ”super-university”.

The new London and South East University Group, to be known as LASE, has more than 50,000 students and four campuses across London, Medway and Kent, and has become the third largest university in the UK.

The two universities will still operate as distinct academic divisions within the university group, retaining their current names.

Students will still apply to and graduate from the institution that they pick.

The higher education institutions announced plans to merge in September last year. The official launch will take place on 7 September, exactly one year on.

It comes as universities in the UK have been facing increasing financial pressures, with MPs on the Education Committee warning earlier this year that there is a “real risk” a university in England could close due to insolvency for the first time.

The Office for Students (OfS), the higher education regulator in England, told the committee that it fears 24 providers are at risk of becoming insolvent and closing in the 12 months from November last year, and warned 45 per cent of higher education providers could be facing a deficit for 2025/26.

The universities of Greenwich and Kent said previously that their merged group will provide a strong financial foundation for getting through economic challenges and would be a “blueprint for others to follow”.

In May, King’s College London and Cranfield University, based in Bedford, announced plans to merge in August 2027.

University of Greenwich vice-chancellor and new chief executive of LASE Professor Jane Harrington said: “There has been tireless work over the last year working to an ambitious timetable and developing a new university model that has never been done before.

“It means we are starting with a smooth transition, an extremely strong senior executive team and clear direction so that we can fulfil our potential as the UK’s first super-university.”
